classes.name: Folketingsvalg
classes.finest_note: Statistics Denmark publishes results by polling district (afstemningsområde) from 2007; earlier volumes report by nomination district, municipality, and (before 1918) single-member constituency.
classes.note: Lower house of the Rigsdag from 1849 to 1953, then the single chamber. Single-member constituencies (open voting by show of hands until 1901) until 1915; proportional representation from 1920. Today 175 members in Denmark (135 constituency and 40 compensatory seats in 10 multi-member constituencies) plus 2 each from the Faroe Islands and Greenland, which their own censuses list.

cadence.vacancy_rule: Folketingsvalgloven § 85: a vacancy passes to the substitute (stedfortræder) on the member's party list; no by-elections.

classes.note: The Rigsråd legislated for the common affairs of Denmark and the duchies. Under the 1863 constitution its Folkething was elected in the Folketing's constituencies by the same rules; its earlier members were partly chosen by the Rigsdag and the duchies' estates and partly elected by the highest taxpayers.

classes.name: Valg til sogneråd, byråd og Borgerrepræsentationen før 1970
classes.name_en: Parish, town, and Copenhagen council elections before 1970
classes.note: Elected parish boards (sogneforstanderskaber, sogneråd from 1867) and town councils (byråd); universal suffrage and proportional representation from the 1908 municipal act, with elections every four years in March from 1909 to 1966.

dates.note: Quadrennial municipal elections from 1909 to 1966 (none in 1941, postponed to 1943); dates and council counts not yet listed from an official source.

classes.name: Kommunale folkeafstemninger
classes.note: Binding municipal referendums under chapter 11 a of the municipal and regional elections act (from 2019), and advisory votes a council calls on its own (such as the 2004-2005 merger votes and Bornholm's 2001 vote). Regions cannot hold them.

access.evidence: Each municipality runs and publishes its own referendums; the ministry describes the rules but keeps no list of votes or results.

classes.name: Valg til ældreråd
classes.note: Every municipality has at least one senior citizens' council of at least 5 members, elected directly at least every four years by residents aged 60 and over, without lists (Ældrelov § 34; earlier retssikkerhedsloven § 30, from 1997).
classes.disposition_reason: Each municipality sets its own rules and runs its own vote, often by post or with the municipal election; no authority compiles the returns.

classes.name: Menighedsrådsvalg
classes.note: Members of the Church of Denmark elect a council in each parish every four years under lov om valg til menighedsråd; most parishes settle the seats at an election meeting (valgforsamling) and only contested parishes hold a ballot.
classes.disposition_reason: Run by each parish's election board; the Ministry of Ecclesiastical Affairs publishes no returns by parish, and its site refused automated requests on 16 November 2026.

classes.name: Valg til skolebestyrelser
classes.note: Parents elect the majority of each municipal school's board; the council sets the election rules (folkeskoleloven § 43).
classes.disposition_reason: The electorate is the parents of one school's pupils, not a public electorate, and schools publish no returns.

classes.name: Dommere og lægdommere
classes.note: No judicial office is elected.
classes.disposition_reason: Judges are appointed by the Crown on the Judicial Appointments Council's recommendation; lay judges and jurors are drawn by lot from lists that municipal committees compile.

classes.name: Opstilling af kandidater
classes.note: Parties nominate candidates internally; independents need voter declarations (folketingsvalgloven § 33).
classes.disposition_reason: Denmark holds no state-run primaries or nominating contests.

classes.name: Indirekte valg
classes.note: Mayors and their deputies and committee chairs (by the municipal council), regional council chairs, the Speaker of the Folketing, county councils before 1970 (chosen by electors from the parish and town councils), Hovedstadsrådet (1974-1989) and Hovedstadens Udviklingsråd (2000-2006), whose members the councils of the capital area chose, and bishops (elected by parish council members and clergy).
classes.disposition_reason: Chosen by elected bodies or by office holders, not by a popular vote; the Prime Minister is appointed by the Monarch and the head of state is hereditary.
